source.title_on_document: Humans Introduce, Models Elaborate: Asymmetric Narrative Agency in Human–LLM Co-Writing

supplement.holds: Recruitment and preprocessing; generation and scoring configuration; qualitative examples and diagnostic figures; turn-level valence descriptives in Table 7; full per-story novelty, transience and resonance asymmetry estimates, confidence intervals and Cliff’s δ in Table 8.

paper_design_summary: A matched corpus comparison reuses Human–LLM (HA) stories from Fundal and Bizzoni (2026), adds a separately recruited Human–Human (HH) cohort that excludes HA participants, and adds LLM–LLM (AA) simulations (p. 12, Appendix A.1). The paper reports 97 HA participants and 72 HH participants who alternated narrative continuations under the same storytelling instructions (p. 3, §3.1). Computational scoring measures turn-level contextual novelty and narrative influence, with additional comparisons of the absolute difference between co-writers’ mean scores within each story (pp. 5–6, §4.4).

studies.label: Matched comparison of Human–Human, Human–LLM and LLM–LLM storytelling corpora

assignment.what_was_assigned: Partner type was determined by corpus membership: the Human–LLM condition was drawn from an earlier study, whereas Human–Human participants were separately recruited and prior HA participants were excluded. HH participants were paired anonymously within the writing interface. This is a comparison of separately assembled cohorts, not a reported random allocation between AI and human partners. Allocation among the different LLM models is not stated.
assignment.quote: The Human–LLM condition is drawn from Fundal and Bizzoni (2026). [...] Participants from the HA experiment were excluded from the Human–Human condition.
assignment.locator: p. 12, Appendix A.1, Recruitment and Preprocessing; corroborated by p. 3, §3.1.

arms.name: Human–LLM (HA)
arms.description: Existing human–LLM co-writing cohort from Fundal and Bizzoni (2026): 97 participants and 97 stories in the final corpus (p. 3, §3.1 and Table 1).

arms.name: Human–Human (HH)
arms.description: Separately recruited human co-writers paired anonymously; 72 participants contributed 36 stories. Earlier HA participants were excluded (p. 3, §3.1 and Table 1; p. 12, Appendix A.1).

arms.name: LLM–LLM (AA)
arms.description: Model-only simulation with two instances of the same model continuing each story; Table 1 reports 80 stories, not a human participant count (p. 3, §3.1 and Table 1). People counts are not applicable.

participants.exclusions: Incomplete sessions, empty turns, and malformed outputs were removed before analysis (p. 3, §3.2; p. 12, Appendix A.1). Stories with missing turns contributed only valid adjacent exchange pairs. Prior HA participants were excluded from HH recruitment (p. 12, Appendix A.1). Turn-level analyses drop turns with missing scores, and transience is undefined for the final exchange of each story (p. 3, Table 1 caption). Initial recruitment counts and the numbers of people removed are not reported.
participants.who: Adult participants recruited from a university context in Denmark, mostly students. HH participants were from English-taught university and graduate programs at Aarhus University. The paper separately reports 97 HA participants and 72 HH participants (p. 3, §3.1); it does not print an aggregate analyzed-person count. Appendix A.1 states that HA participants were excluded from HH, establishing that these cohorts do not overlap.
participants.quote: There were 97 participants [...] The HH condition used the same turn-taking structure as the HA condition and included 72 participants
participants.locator: p. 3, §§3.1–3.2 and Table 1 (arm counts, final analytic corpus and filtering); p. 10, Limitations and Ethics Statement (population and Denmark); p. 12, Appendix A.1 (recruitment, non-overlap and preprocessing).

ai_tool.how_used: An LLM served as an alternating narrative co-writer in HA; paired instances of the same model generated AA stories. All conditions used the same collaborative storytelling instructions. Human contributions in the analytic corpus were subsequently spell-corrected with gpt-4o-mini before scoring; this was preprocessing rather than assistance while HH participants wrote (p. 3, §3.1; p. 12, Appendix A.1–A.2).

task.description: Open-ended collaborative storytelling in English: alternate contributions and continue where the partner left off, under an instruction allowing 10 exchanges. The analyzed HA stories contained 9 full exchanges. No elapsed task duration is stated (p. 3, §3.1–3.2; p. 10, Ethics Statement).

outcomes.name: Novelty asymmetry between co-writers: absolute difference between their mean turn scores within a story
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Novelty is contextual minus context-free (beginning-of-sequence) mean token surprisal, scored with google/gemma-4-31B; less negative values indicate greater contextual novelty (p. 5, §4.4, Eqs. (4)–(5)). The analyzed outcome is the per-story absolute difference between the two writer slots’ mean scores (p. 6, §4.4, Eq. (7); p. 15, Table 8). Higher values indicate a larger co-writer gap, without establishing higher overall story creativity. The paper reports bootstrap confidence intervals and Cliff’s δ (p. 10, Limitations; p. 15, Table 8). The intervals describe arm means; Cliff’s δ is a rank-based between-arm effect, not a standardized mean difference. Robustness information: the shuffled-context HA check used google/gemma-4-12B; the main scorer was google/gemma-4-31B. Additional checks examined length-controlled lexical overlap, surface novelty and length, other surface metrics, and scorer familiarity across generator families (pp. 8–9, Robustness and Permutation and subsequent checks).

contrasts.reported: HA versus HH, per-story novelty asymmetry A_m: HA mean 0.828, 95% CI [0.732, 0.926], n = 97 stories; HH mean 0.355, 95% CI [0.284, 0.428], n = 36 stories. Table 8 reports Cliff’s δ = 0.591 for HA against HH. These are differences between writer slots within each story, not mean creativity ratings of the stories.
contrasts.locator: p. 15, Table 8, Novelty rows and caption; pp. 5–6, §4.4 and Eq. (7) (definition and surprisal scoring).

outcomes.name: Contextual novelty of human versus LLM turns within Human–LLM stories
outcomes.question: none

This comparison distinguishes human and LLM author roles within HA stories; it does not estimate the effect of assistance on human output. Robustness information: the shuffled-context HA check used google/gemma-4-12B; the main scorer was google/gemma-4-31B. Additional checks examined length-controlled lexical overlap, surface novelty and length, other surface metrics, and scorer familiarity across generator families (pp. 8–9, Robustness and Permutation and subsequent checks).

contrasts.reported: Within HA, human turns: mean Novelty = −1.82, with 30.2% of turn-information explained by prior context; LLM turns: mean Novelty = −2.65, with 52.8% explained; p < .0001. Novelty is contextual minus context-free mean token surprisal, scored with google/gemma-4-31B; less negative values indicate greater contextual novelty. This contrast compares the two co-writer roles within HA, not people assigned to different assistance conditions.
contrasts.locator: p. 7, §5.3, paragraph beginning 'Humans contribute higher novelty and resonance in HA stories'; p. 5, §4.4, Eq. (5) (measure).

outcomes.name: Resonance asymmetry between co-writers: absolute difference between their mean narrative-influence scores within a story
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Novelty is contextual minus context-free (beginning-of-sequence) mean token surprisal, scored with google/gemma-4-31B; less negative values indicate greater contextual novelty (p. 5, §4.4, Eqs. (4)–(5)). Transience is the mean surprisal of the immediately following counterpart turn with the current turn added to prior context minus its mean surprisal given prior context alone, using google/gemma-4-31B; more negative values indicate stronger predictive uptake (p. 5, §4.4, Eq. (6)). Resonance is novelty minus transience, indicating whether contextually surprising material predicts the following contribution (p. 5, §4.4). The analyzed outcome is the per-story absolute difference between the two writer slots’ mean scores (p. 6, §4.4, Eq. (7); p. 15, Table 8). Higher values indicate a larger co-writer gap, without establishing higher overall story creativity. The paper reports bootstrap confidence intervals and Cliff’s δ (p. 10, Limitations; p. 15, Table 8). The intervals describe arm means; Cliff’s δ is a rank-based between-arm effect, not a standardized mean difference. Robustness information: the shuffled-context HA check used google/gemma-4-12B; the main scorer was google/gemma-4-31B. Additional checks examined length-controlled lexical overlap, surface novelty and length, other surface metrics, and scorer familiarity across generator families (pp. 8–9, Robustness and Permutation and subsequent checks).

contrasts.reported: HA versus HH, per-story resonance asymmetry A_m: HA mean 1.290, 95% CI [1.149, 1.432], n = 97 stories; HH mean 0.605, 95% CI [0.482, 0.733], n = 36 stories. Table 8 reports Cliff’s δ = 0.572 for HA against HH. Resonance is novelty minus transience, measuring whether contextually surprising material predicts the following contribution; the reported outcome is the absolute difference between co-writers’ mean resonance, not an overall creativity score.

outcomes.name: Predictive uptake of human contributions with an LLM versus a human partner
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Transience is the mean surprisal of the immediately following counterpart turn with the current turn added to prior context minus its mean surprisal given prior context alone, using google/gemma-4-31B; more negative values indicate stronger predictive uptake (p. 5, §4.4, Eq. (6)). Predictive uptake is the normalized surprisal reduction: minus transience divided by the baseline mean surprisal of the future turn given prior context, expressed as a percentage (pp. 5–6, §4.4). Table 3 reports story-level clustered means for directed turns after the first turn. The responding partner determines the target text being scored. Raw transience is retained alongside its normalized uptake variant; higher uptake corresponds to more negative transience. Robustness information: the shuffled-context HA check used google/gemma-4-12B; the main scorer was google/gemma-4-31B. Additional checks examined length-controlled lexical overlap, surface novelty and length, other surface metrics, and scorer familiarity across generator families (pp. 8–9, Robustness and Permutation and subsequent checks).

contrasts.treatment_arm: Human contributions followed by LLM responses in Human–LLM (HA) stories
contrasts.control_arm: Human contributions followed by human responses in Human–Human (HH) stories
contrasts.reported: Human → AI (HA): baseline future-turn surprisal 3.39 bits/token; transience −1.02; normalized uptake 30.0%. Human → Human (HH): baseline future-turn surprisal 4.78 bits/token; transience −0.83; normalized uptake 17.2%. Table 3 describes all values as story-level clustered means. The text reports 12.8 percentage points more uptake for human contributions with an LLM partner. No interval, standard error, or p-value is supplied for this partner contrast. The direction field describes normalized uptake.
contrasts.locator: p. 8, Table 3, Human → AI and Human → Human rows and caption; p. 7, §5.3, paragraph beginning “Keeping speaker”; pp. 5–6, §4.4 (definition).

outcomes.name: Novelty–resonance coupling by co-writing condition
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Novelty is contextual minus context-free (beginning-of-sequence) mean token surprisal, scored with google/gemma-4-31B; less negative values indicate greater contextual novelty (p. 5, §4.4, Eqs. (4)–(5)). Transience is the mean surprisal of the immediately following counterpart turn with the current turn added to prior context minus its mean surprisal given prior context alone, using google/gemma-4-31B; more negative values indicate stronger predictive uptake (p. 5, §4.4, Eq. (6)). Resonance is novelty minus transience, indicating whether contextually surprising material predicts the following contribution (p. 5, §4.4). Resonance is regressed on novelty, condition, and their interaction with a story-level random intercept; observations are turn outputs. The reported condition-specific slopes measure novelty–resonance coupling (p. 6, §4.4, Modeling). Robustness information: the shuffled-context HA check used google/gemma-4-12B; the main scorer was google/gemma-4-31B. Additional checks examined length-controlled lexical overlap, surface novelty and length, other surface metrics, and scorer familiarity across generator families (pp. 8–9, Robustness and Permutation and subsequent checks).

contrasts.reported: Novelty–resonance slope: HA 1.217, 95% CI [1.184, 1.250]; HH 1.066, 95% CI [1.003, 1.128]. The model-only AA reference slope is 0.956, 95% CI [0.913, 0.999]. These are condition-specific slopes and intervals, not a reported HA-minus-HH slope difference or its interval.
contrasts.locator: p. 7, §5.3, “Novelty couples with resonance in HA stories,” and Figure 4; p. 6, §4.4, Modeling.

outcomes.name: Local semantic distance between adjacent co-writer turns
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Cosine distance between adjacent turn embeddings from Kingsoft-LLM/QZhou-Embedding. The mixed model uses adjacent-pair distance as the outcome, condition as a fixed effect, and a story-level random intercept (pp. 4–5, §4.3, Eq. (3)). This measures local dissimilarity within a jointly written story. It does not compare independent writers’ output sets and is therefore coded other, with_ai rather than diversity, across_people. The paper also displays story-level distance diagnostics (p. 14, Figure 12).

contrasts.reported: Adjacent semantic distance: HA mean 0.316 versus HH mean 0.287; mixed-model HA minus HH Δ = 0.0299, p < .0001. The model-only AA reference mean is 0.296; the separately reported HA minus AA contrast is Δ = 0.0198, p < .0001. HA versus the average of HH and AA: Δ = 0.0248, p < .0001. The latter contrasts include a model-only baseline.
contrasts.locator: p. 6, §5.2, “HA exchanges show high semantic distance”; p. 7, Figure 3; pp. 4–5, §4.3 (measure and model).

outcomes.question: none
outcomes.measure_detail: Transience is the mean surprisal of the immediately following counterpart turn with the current turn added to prior context minus its mean surprisal given prior context alone, using google/gemma-4-31B; more negative values indicate stronger predictive uptake (p. 5, §4.4, Eq. outcomes.name: Difference in novelty–resonance coupling between author roles within Human–LLM stories
outcomes.question: none
outcomes.measure_detail: Novelty is contextual minus context-free (beginning-of-sequence) mean token surprisal, scored with google/gemma-4-31B; less negative values indicate greater contextual novelty (p. 5, §4.4, Eqs. (4)–(5)). Transience is the mean surprisal of the immediately following counterpart turn with the current turn added to prior context minus its mean surprisal given prior context alone, using google/gemma-4-31B; more negative values indicate stronger predictive uptake (p. 5, §4.4, Eq. eligibility.reason: Criterion 1 is not met: the text specifies reuse of a prior HA cohort and separate HH recruitment excluding prior HA participants, establishing a non-random comparison of cohorts (p. 12, Appendix A.1; p. 3, §3.1). Random assignment among LLM configurations is not reported either. Criterion 2 is met by the separately reported 97 HA participants and 72 HH participants; either human cohort exceeds the threshold. The paper does not print an aggregate analyzed-person count, so that field is null (p. 3, §3.1 and Table 1; p. 12, Appendix A.1). Criterion 3 is met because contextual novelty is computed on produced story turns (p. 5, §4.4). The HA-versus-HH comparisons remain observational context. Within-HA author-role contrasts are coded question none, and local adjacent-turn semantic distance is not coded as diversity across independent writers. The paper does not enter the core randomized dataset.

one_line_finding: In this non-random corpus comparison, novelty asymmetry was larger in human–LLM than human–human stories (0.828 versus 0.355; p. 15, Table 8), and within human–LLM stories human turns were more novel than LLM turns (−1.82 versus −2.65, p < .0001; p. 7, §5.3).
notes: The repository URLs are those printed in the PDF; their current availability and contents were not checked (p. 3, footnote 1; p. 12, Appendix A.2). Narrative-influence and local semantic-distance outcomes are recorded as process measures, with within-HA author-role comparisons identified separately. Pure affective valence/alignment measures and illustrative excerpts are outside the creativity/diversity questions. Surface-metric and shuffled-context checks are retained as robustness information in measure_detail (pp. 4–9; Appendix A). Score-specific observation totals are not inferred from Table 1 or the valence counts in Table 7. For descriptive-only contrasts, statistics_available is ["none"] because no applicable SD/SE/CI/test flag is supported; the printed means remain in reported.
